title: Eliminating an inverse equation from local Koszul generators
statement: Let $A$ be a commutative ring, $I\subseteq A$ an ideal, $\mathfrak q\subset A$ a prime ideal containing $I$, and $h\in A\setminus\mathfrak q$. In the one-variable polynomial ring $B=A[z]$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring], put $J=IB+(hz-1)$ and $\mathfrak q' = \mathfrak q B+(hz-1)$, the prime ideal with quotient $(A/\mathfrak q)[1/\overline h]$. Suppose there are $v\in B\setminus\mathfrak q'$, $e\geq0$, and $b_1,\ldots,b_e\in B_v$ such that $JB_v=(b_1,\ldots,b_e)$ and $H_i(K_\bullet(B_v;b_1,\ldots,b_e))=0$ for all $i>0$. Then there are $d\in A\setminus\mathfrak q$, $r\geq0$, and $f_1,\ldots,f_r\in A_d$ such that $IA_d=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ and $H_i(K_\bullet(A_d;f_1,\ldots,f_r))=0$ for all $i>0$. All localizations are at powers of the displayed element [def-weil-ring-localization-away]; the displayed homology vanishing is Koszul regularity [def-weil-pbc-koszul-regular-sequence]. No finite-generation hypothesis on $I$, no Noetherian hypothesis on $A$, and no flatness hypothesis are imposed.

source.place: Tag 07D1 (lemma-lci-local), local subargument from the prime (q, x_{n+1}h_j-1) to the final principal neighbourhood h-prime: selecting conormal generators, replacing equal-length generators, and removing the inverse equation. The ring called R[x_1,...,x_n] there is here an arbitrary commutative ring A; the argument uses no further property of that ring.

proof.text: Put $t=hz-1$, $R=B_v$, $L=JR$ and $K=tR\subseteq L$. Multiplication by $t$ is injective on $B$: if $(hz-1)\sum a_i z^i=0$, its coefficients give $a_0=0$ and $a_i=ha_{i-1}=0$ successively. It is also injective on $R$: $t(p/v^m)=0$ implies $tv^np=0$ in $B$ for some $n$, hence $v^np=0$ and $p/v^m=0$. The one-element Koszul complex is $[R\xrightarrow{t}R]$ in degrees $1,0$, so $(t)$ is Koszul-regular. The given tuple $(b_1,\ldots,b_e)$ generates $L$ and is Koszul-regular. Thus both ideals satisfy the local-generation hypothesis of the cancellation lemma, at every prime over $L$, by taking the localization element $1$. Also $K$ is finitely generated, and $R/L\xrightarrow{\sim}K/KL$, $\bar a\mapsto\overline{ta}$, is an isomorphism by the injectivity of multiplication by $t$.

proof.text: The conormal sequence for $K\subseteq L$ is split exact by an explicit calculation. In the ring $R[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$, substitution $z\mapsto z(1+\epsilon)$ and fixing $A$ sends $v$ to $v+\epsilon z v^{\prime}$, with inverse $v^{-1}-\epsilon z v^{\prime}v^{-2}$; it therefore defines a map $R\to R[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$. Write this map as $x\mapsto x+\epsilon\delta(x)$. Multiplicativity gives $\delta(xy)=x\delta(y)+y\delta(x)$, and $\delta(t)=hz\equiv1\pmod L$. Thus $[x]\mapsto\overline{t\delta(x)}$ defines an $R/L$-linear map $\rho:L/L^2\to K/KL$: the product rule kills $L^2$ modulo $L$, and also gives linearity modulo $L$. For $x=ta$ it gives $\rho([ta])=\overline{ta}$ since $t\in L$ and $\delta(t)\equiv1\pmod L$. Consequently $\rho\alpha=1$, where $\alpha:K/KL\to L/L^2$ is inclusion. The remaining exactness is the identity $\ker(L/L^2\to L/(K+L^2))=(K+L^2)/L^2=\operatorname{im}\alpha$.

proof.text: The ideal $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q^{\prime}R$ is prime and contains $L$: indeed $R/\mathfrak p=((A/\mathfrak q)_{\bar h})_{\bar v}$ is a nonzero domain since $v\notin\mathfrak q^{\prime}$. Apply [lem-sfb-koszul-split-conormal-cancellation] with the ideals $K\subseteq L$ in $R$ and the prime $\mathfrak p/K$ of $C=R/K$. Steps 1 and 2 verify every hypothesis, including finite generation of $K$ and the split exact sequence. It supplies $u\in C\setminus(\mathfrak p/K)$ and a finite Koszul-regular tuple generating $(L/K)C_u$.

Evaluation $z\mapsto h^{-1}$ identifies $B/(t)$ with $A_h$: its inverse sends $h^{-1}$ to $z$, and the two composites fix $A,z,h^{-1}$. Hence $C=(A_h)_{w}$ with $w=v(h^{-1})$. Write $w=c/h^N$ with $c\in A$; $c

Its generated ideal is $IA_d$, and the coefficientwise isomorphism of its Koszul complexes carries kernels and images bijectively, preserving the positive homology vanishing. This proves both required clauses, allowing $r=0$.
